concepts.topicTitle: DNA Copying and the Importance of Variation in Reproduction
concepts.label: DNA Copying: The Basic Event of Reproduction
concepts.cardText: Organisms look similar because their body designs are similar, so the blueprints for those designs must be similar too. Reproduction at its most basic level therefore means making copies of the blueprints of body design. The chromosomes in the nucleus contain information for inheritance in the form of DNA molecules, and DNA is the information source for making proteins. If the information changes, different proteins are made and body designs alter. So a basic event in reproduction is the creation of a DNA copy. The two copies are separated along with an additional cellular apparatus, and the cell divides into two. Because no biochemical reaction is absolutely reliable, the copies are similar but may not be identical.

concepts.topicTitle: DNA Copying and the Importance of Variation in Reproduction
concepts.label: The Importance of Variation
concepts.cardText: Populations of organisms fill well-defined places, or niches, in the ecosystem using their ability to reproduce. Consistency of DNA copying maintains the body design features that suit a niche, so reproduction is linked to the stability of populations. But niches can change for reasons beyond the organisms' control: temperatures rise or fall, water levels vary, or meteorites hit. If a population suited to a niche were drastically changed it could be wiped out; but if some variations are present in a few individuals, there is a chance for them to survive. If bacteria in temperate water face global warming, most die but the few heat-resistant variants survive and grow. Variation is useful for survival of the species over time.

concepts.topicTitle: Asexual Reproduction Modes: Fission, Fragmentation, Regeneration and Budding
concepts.label: Fission in Single-celled Organisms
concepts.cardText: The modes by which organisms reproduce depend on their body design. For unicellular organisms, cell division, or fission, creates new individuals. Many bacteria and protozoa simply split into two equal halves; in Amoeba the split can happen in any plane. Leishmania, which causes kala-azar, has a whip-like structure at one end and divides by binary fission in a definite orientation to it. The malarial parasite Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells simultaneously by multiple fission. Yeast puts out small buds that separate and grow further.

concepts.topicTitle: Asexual Reproduction Modes: Fission, Fragmentation, Regeneration and Budding
concepts.label: Fragmentation and Why Complex Organisms Cannot Divide Cell by Cell
concepts.cardText: In multi-cellular organisms with relatively simple body organisation, simple reproductive methods can still work. Spirogyra simply breaks up into smaller pieces upon maturation, and these fragments grow into new individuals. This is not true for all multi-cellular organisms, which cannot simply divide cell by cell. Specialised cells are organised as tissues, and tissues as organs placed at definite positions in the body, so cell-by-cell division would be impractical. They need more complex ways of reproduction, so reproduction is the function of a specific cell type capable of growing, proliferating and making other cell types under the right circumstances.

concepts.topicTitle: Asexual Reproduction Modes: Fission, Fragmentation, Regeneration and Budding
concepts.label: Regeneration and Budding
concepts.cardText: Many fully differentiated organisms can give rise to new individuals from their body parts: simple animals such as Hydra and Planaria can be cut into any number of pieces and each grows into a complete organism. This is regeneration. It is carried out by specialised cells that proliferate and make large numbers of cells, which then change into various cell types and tissues in an organised sequence called development. Regeneration is not the same as reproduction, since most organisms would not normally depend on being cut up to reproduce. In budding, Hydra uses regenerative cells for reproduction: a bud develops as an outgrowth due to repeated cell division at one specific site, grows into a tiny individual and detaches when mature.

concepts.label: Vegetative Propagation: Growing New Plants from Plant Parts
concepts.cardText: In many plants, parts like the root, stem and leaves develop into new plants under appropriate conditions. Unlike most animals, plants can use this mode for reproduction. Vegetative propagation is used in methods such as layering or grafting to grow plants like sugarcane, roses or grapes. Plants raised by it can bear flowers and fruits earlier than those from seeds, and it makes possible the propagation of plants such as banana, orange, rose and jasmine that have lost the capacity to produce seeds. All plants produced are genetically similar enough to the parent to have all its characteristics. Examples include buds in the notches of potato and the Bryophyllum leaf margin, and tissue culture.

concepts.label: Spore Formation and Asexual Reproduction
concepts.cardText: Even in many simple multi-cellular organisms, specific reproductive parts can be identified. The thread-like hyphae seen on the bread mould Rhizopus are not reproductive parts. The tiny blob-on-a-stick structures are, and the blobs are sporangia, which contain cells called spores that can eventually develop into new Rhizopus individuals. The spores are covered by thick walls that protect them until they come into contact with another moist surface and can begin to grow. All the modes so far allow new generations to be created from a single individual, which is known as asexual reproduction.

concepts.topicTitle: Significance of Sexual Reproduction and Meiotic Chromosome Reduction
concepts.label: Why Sexual Reproduction? Generating More Variation
concepts.cardText: Sexual reproduction needs two individuals, males and females. The DNA copying mechanism cannot be absolutely accurate, and the resulting errors are a source of variation. Variation cannot protect every individual, but in a population it helps ensure the survival of the species. Copying errors make the generation of variation a fairly slow process. Each variation is made in a DNA copy that already has variations accumulated from previous generations, so two individuals have quite different patterns of accumulated variations. Combining variations from two or more individuals creates new combinations, each novel because it involves two individuals. The sexual mode of reproduction incorporates this combining of DNA from two different individuals.

concepts.topicTitle: Significance of Sexual Reproduction and Meiotic Chromosome Reduction
concepts.label: Meiosis, Germ-cells and the Male and Female Gametes
concepts.cardText: Combining DNA from two individuals creates a difficulty: each generation would have twice the amount of DNA of the previous one, which would mess up the control of the cellular apparatus. Many multi-cellular organisms solve this with special lineages of cells in specialised organs having only half the number of chromosomes and half the DNA of non-reproductive body cells, produced by a cell division called meiosis. When germ-cells from two individuals combine, the number of chromosomes and DNA content is re-established. As body designs become more complex, germ-cells specialise: one large and with food stores, the other smaller and motile. The motile one is the male gamete and the one with stored food the female gamete.

concepts.label: Parts of a Flower and the Germ-cells
concepts.cardText: The reproductive parts of angiosperms are in the flower, whose parts are sepals, petals, stamens and pistil. Stamens and pistil are the reproductive parts containing the germ-cells. A flower is unisexual (papaya, watermelon) if it has either stamens or pistil, and bisexual (Hibiscus, mustard) if it has both. The stamen is the male part and produces yellowish pollen grains. The pistil, in the centre, is the female part, made of the swollen ovary at the bottom, the elongated style in the middle and the sometimes sticky stigma at the top. The ovary contains ovules, and each ovule has an egg cell.

concepts.label: Pollination, Fertilisation and Seed Formation
concepts.cardText: The male germ-cell from the pollen grain fuses with the female gamete in the ovule; this fusion is fertilisation, and it gives the zygote that can grow into a new plant. The pollen must therefore be transferred from the stamen to the stigma. If this happens in the same flower it is self-pollination; if from one flower to another it is cross-pollination, achieved by wind, water or animals. After the pollen lands on a suitable stigma, a tube grows out of the pollen grain through the style to reach the ovary. After fertilisation the zygote divides to form an embryo within the ovule. The ovule develops a tough coat and becomes a seed, while the ovary ripens into a fruit. The seed's embryo develops into a seedling by germination.

concepts.topicTitle: Human Puberty and Secondary Sexual Characteristics
concepts.label: Changes at Puberty
concepts.cardText: Growth makes the body larger, but in early teenage years the appearance of the body changes in ways that cannot be explained by enlargement alone. Some changes are common to boys and girls: thick hair in new parts of the body such as armpits and the genital area, oily skin with pimples, and a new awareness of bodies. Girls' breast size begins to increase and they begin to menstruate; boys get thick facial hair and their voices crack. The changes are slow, take months and years, and vary between people in timing and pattern. They are aspects of sexual maturation. While the body is growing to adult size its resources go mainly to growth, so as general growth slows, reproductive tissues mature; this period of adolescence is called puberty. Many changes signal maturity to others.

concepts.topicTitle: Human Male and Female Reproductive Systems and Fertilisation
concepts.label: The Human Male Reproductive System and Sperm Transport
concepts.cardText: The male reproductive system consists of portions that produce germ-cells and portions that deliver them to the site of fertilisation. Sperms are formed in the testes, located outside the abdominal cavity in the scrotum because sperm formation requires a lower temperature than normal body temperature. The testes also secrete the hormone testosterone, which regulates the formation of sperms and brings about the changes of puberty. Sperms are delivered through the vas deferens, which unites with a tube from the urinary bladder, so the urethra is a common passage for sperms and urine. Glands such as the prostate and the seminal vesicles add secretions so the sperms are in a fluid which makes transport easier and provides nutrition. Sperms are tiny, mainly genetic material with a long tail for movement.

concepts.topicTitle: Human Male and Female Reproductive Systems and Fertilisation
concepts.label: The Female Reproductive System, Fertilisation and Development of the Embryo
concepts.cardText: Eggs are made in the ovaries, which also produce some hormones. A girl is born with thousands of immature eggs in the ovaries; at puberty some start maturing and one egg is produced each month by one of the ovaries. The egg is carried through the oviduct (fallopian tube) to the uterus, which opens into the vagina through the cervix. Sperms enter the vagina and travel up to the oviduct where they may meet the egg. The zygote divides into a ball of cells, the embryo, which is implanted in the uterine lining and grows into a foetus. The embryo gets nutrition from the mother's blood through the placenta, a disc embedded in the uterine wall with villi on the embryo's side. Wastes pass back to the mother's blood. Development takes about nine months and birth happens through rhythmic contractions of the uterus.

concepts.topicTitle: Menstrual Cycle and Reproductive Health: Contraception
concepts.label: Menstruation: When the Egg Is Not Fertilised
concepts.cardText: If the egg is not fertilised, it lives for about one day. Since the ovary releases one egg every month, the uterus also prepares itself every month to receive a fertilised egg, and its lining becomes thick and spongy and richly supplied with blood. This would be needed to nourish an embryo if fertilisation had taken place. When it is not, the lining is no longer needed, so it slowly breaks and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucous. This cycle takes place roughly every month and is known as menstruation. It usually lasts about two to eight days.

concepts.topicTitle: Menstrual Cycle and Reproductive Health: Contraception
concepts.label: Reproductive Health, Sexually Transmitted Infections and Contraception
concepts.cardText: Sexual maturation is gradual and takes place while general body growth is still going on, so some maturation does not mean the body or mind is ready for sexual acts or for bringing up children. Many diseases can be sexually transmitted, including gonorrhoea and syphilis (bacterial) and warts and HIV-AIDS (viral). A condom helps prevent transmission of many of these to some extent. Contraceptive methods avoid pregnancy: mechanical barriers such as condoms, hormonal pills that stop eggs being released, devices such as the loop or copper-T placed in the uterus, and surgical methods blocking the vas deferens or the fallopian tube. Each has possible side-effects. Sex-selective abortion of female foetuses is illegal and declines the child sex ratio.
